newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EMU worries continue over German debt, jobs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMU worries continue over German debt, jobs.

text.p: Worries persisted on Thursday over Germany's ability to qualify for the single currency as it emerged that the European Commission expected the country's debt to remain high and its unemployment problems to fester.

Adding fuel to talk of a postponement of economic and monetary union (EMU) from its January 1999 target, a poll of Germans showed a big majority favouring a delay if the alternative was fudging or weakening the rules of entry.

But a poll of market analysts conducted by Reuters found most still believed the project would start on time, and the European commissioner for monetary affairs again ruled out either a delay or a change in the qualifying criteria.

Good news for EMU came from the Commission, which, a source said, had concluded after studying France's latest economic convergence plan that the country was on track to bring its deficit to 3.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product this year.
That is the key criteria and one which is proving the hardest to meet in many EU capitals.

But the source told Reuters that having studied Germany's plan the Commission believed that Bonn's debt would remain above 60 percent of GDP, potentially ruling out Germany depending on how the EU chooses to evaluate its own rules.
The source also said the Commission was decidedly pessimistic about the chances of Germany quickly bringing down its unemployment rate.
Record jobless queues are hampering Bonn's ability to cut its deficit or its debt ahead of monetary union.
Such difficulties -- matched by concerns in Germany itself that fudging the criteria would be to invite lesser economies also to qualify -- have led to widespread talk of a delay in EMU.
Echoing the firm stance taken by France and Germany on Wednesday, however, EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy rejected any talk of delay or fudge.
"There is no question about changing the criteria or changing the date," he told a briefing with Swedish reporters in Brussels.
He added that he expected several countries to be ready for monetary union on time, referring in particular to Commission projections for EU growth at 2.3 percent for 1997.
Growth at that rate, along with the potential for further export-led growth fuelled by the rising dollar, would help countries lower their debt to GDP ratio by raising GDP.
Apart from EU officials, meanwhile, opinions varied over the question of an EMU delay.
A Reuter poll of analysts suggested that the chances of monetary union going ahead on time were still high, despite slippage over German worries.

In the survey, carried out between March 10 and 11, the mean of 45 forecasts showed that the average likelihood of economic and monetary union (EMU) going ahead on its scheduled launch date of January 1, 1999 had fallen to 76 percent, from 83 percent in February and January and 86 percent in December.
But Germans themselves were less sure.
Three-quarters of German voters polled by the Forsa survey in the weekly Die Woche said they believed the euro should be delayed if member countries do not meet the criteria.
A mere 14 percent argued for softening the tough line backed by the Bundesbank central bank and Finance Minister Theo Waigel in order to allow the launch to take place on schedule in 1999.
